newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. troops begin new move to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troops begin new move to Bosnia.

text.p: The first U.S. soldiers assigned to Bosnia as a new "covering force" left Germany on Tuesday with little of the fanfare that sent off earlier U.S. contingents headed for Balkan peacekeeping.

Unlike U.S. troops that left Germany last December for Bosnia with a rousing send-off from President Bill Clinton, soldiers leaving on Tuesday sat around reading newspapers and eating cheeseburgers while waiting for their trains to leave.
Two trains carrying equipment and about 20 soldiers each left Conn barracks near Schweinfurt in southern Germany for a 30-hour journey to staging grounds in Hungary.
Other trains were scheduled to leave Germany throughout the day and night. The troops will collect equipment in Hungary and drive through Croatia to Bosnia, commanders said.
A few hundred more soldiers will leave by bus on Wednesday, followed over two to three weeks by the rest of the 5,000 soldiers of the army's First Infantry Division.
The soldiers are unsure when they will return and some U.S. Congressmen have sharply criticised the deployment as a sign of "mission creep".
The new troops are to help the withdrawal of 15,000 American peacekeepers whose U.N. mandate ends on December 20.

But NATO has been pushing for a follow-on force with a U.S. presence to remain in Bosnia after December, and the pullout date has already slipped by weeks due to delays in municipal elections, which are now set for late November.
The U.S. European Command in Stuttgart said on Tuesday that the number of U.S. troops in the region will peak at about 18,000 in early November -- below the cap of 20,000 U.S. soldiers allowed.
Once the bulk of the "covering force" is in place other U.S. troops will then begin leaving. By the time the U.N. mandate ends the numbers will be down to about 10,000.
When the remainer will leave is unclear.
"They told us we will be back in March but we will have to see what happens and when we can come home," said Specialist Edmund Switzer, 27, of Las Vegas, Nevada.
Switzer said good-bye to his wife at their apartment before joining his unit at the Conn barracks near Schweinfurt.
But Sergeant John Silber took advantage of the last minutes, giving his wife and two sons a last hug and kiss a few minutes before boarding the train.
"I told them that this is my job, how I make a living," said Silber, 29, of Beeville, Texas. "It will be OK. And I promised my sons to take them camping when I get back."
